analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before the government searches Americans' communications or buys their personal data from brokers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 7 cosponsors on March 5, 2026, and referred to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing or vote; it would require warrants for government searches of Americans' communications and ban warrantless purchases of Americans' records from data brokers.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the government can spy. It would bar intelligence analysts from searching a large surveillance database for the communications of Americans without a warrant (with narrow exceptions for emergencies, consent, and cyber defense). It would scale back which businesses can be forced to help the government wiretap, and it would make it harder for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to simply buy Americans' location data and records from data brokers instead of getting a court order. It would also extend the underlying surveillance law (Section 702) to 2028, pairing reauthorization with these limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose phone calls, emails, location data, and browsing records could otherwise be searched or purchased by federal agencies without a warrant. Anyone whose data is collected under FISA's Section 702 program — which sweeps in communications of Americans talking to people overseas — would get a warrant requirement before the government looks for them in that database, and a ban on agencies buying data-broker records that would need a warrant if requested directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people's private communications and data

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal officers from conducting warrantless queries for the communications of United States persons in information acquired under FISA Section 702, with exceptions only for a court order, an emergency involving imminent death or serious bodily harm, consent, or narrowly scoped defensive cybersecurity searches; information from an unauthorized query cannot be used as evidence in any proceeding.

Bars law enforcement agencies and the intelligence community from obtaining customers' records, location information, or illegitimately obtained data from third parties in exchange for anything of value, and blocks such records from being used as evidence; this is the 'Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act' portion of the bill.

Requires a court order, under the most stringent applicable constitutional standard, before the government can compel a third party to hand over covered customer records — closing the pathway of buying from a broker what would require a warrant to demand from a provider directly.

Sunsets the expanded definition of 'electronic communication service provider' on December 31, 2026, narrowing which businesses (beyond phone and internet companies) can be compelled to serve as conduits for government surveillance, and limits directives to certain providers with new FISA Court review and congressional reporting.

Requires the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to appoint a friend-of-the-court adviser with privacy and civil liberties expertise in novel or sensitive cases (including cases involving public officials, political organizations, or the news media), and expands that adviser's access to the government's filings and court opinions.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. intelligence agencies and federal law enforcement, which would lose the ability to search the 702 database for Americans' communications without a warrant and could no longer buy location and records data from brokers. Commercial data brokers would lose government agencies as a paying customer. Communications providers would face some new compliance requirements, though many would gain relief from compelled surveillance assistance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies, law enforcement, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The warrant requirement carries exceptions: queries without a warrant are still allowed in emergencies, with consent, for certain cybersecurity purposes, and for people already under court-authorized surveillance, and emergency-query information can be used in proceedings arising from the threat that prompted the query.

The bill extends FISA Title VII — the Section 702 surveillance authority — to April 20, 2028, meaning it reauthorizes the underlying program for two more years rather than letting it lapse; opponents of 702 itself would view the trade skeptically.

The main penalty for violating the new rules is that illegally obtained information cannot be used as evidence, plus internal minimization procedures and agency reporting to Congress; the bill does not create a private right to sue, so enforcement depends on suppression motions and oversight rather than individual remedies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: the bill gives Americans a warrant requirement before the government searches for them in a database that collects their communications, and stops agencies from end-running the Fourth Amendment by purchasing data from brokers. The costs are modest for most people, though national security agencies argue warrant requirements slow threat detection; the bill's own emergency and cybersecurity exceptions are meant to answer that, while the two-year extension of 702 keeps the underlying collection in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, where it has not received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; Congress is still in session, so its fate is undecided.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ), joined by Reps. Eli Crane and Andrew Clyde, introduced the bill on March 5, 2026, and it gathered 7 Republican cosponsors in total.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence; no further action appears in the record.

The bill would amend FISA to prohibit warrantless queries for the communications of United States persons under Section 702, with exceptions for court orders, emergencies, consent, and certain cybersecurity searches.

Title II of the bill, called the Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act, would bar law enforcement and intelligence agencies from buying Americans' customer records, location data, or illegitimately obtained information from third parties, and would bar such records from use as evidence.
The bill would also extend the repeal date of FISA Title VII to April 20, 2028, effectively reauthorizing the Section 702 program for two more years alongside the new warrant restrictions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything: because no vote has occurred and no law has changed, intelligence agencies continue operating under current warrantless-query rules and data brokers continue selling to the government. If the bill stays buried, those interests are the ones better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and data brokers, so far

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor so far is a House Republican (7 of 223); no Democrat has signed on and no opposition has been recorded, since the bill has not reached a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill bans law enforcement and intelligence agencies from buying covered customer records, location data, or illegitimately obtained information from third parties, cutting off a paying customer for brokered personal data. It also bars such records from use as evidence, reducing the value of that data to agencies.

industries.industry: U.S. intelligence agencies and federal law enforcement
industries.note: Agencies would need a warrant, an emergency, or consent before querying the 702 database for Americans' communications, and could no longer buy location and records data from brokers as a substitute for a court order. The bill pairs this with a two-year extension of the underlying 702 authority, so the program itself survives.

The bill sunsets the expanded definition of electronic communication service provider on December 31, 2026, relieving many businesses beyond telecom carriers of compelled surveillance assistance, while imposing new notification and court-review duties on providers still subject to directives. Most providers gain net flexibility; the public gains privacy.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session. With only 7 cosponsors, a dual referral to two powerful committees, and no committee action on record since introduction, the bill is unlikely to get standalone floor time. Its most realistic path — and the reason it extends 702 to 2028 — is being folded into the broader FISA reauthorization fight around the April 2026 expiration of the current Section 702 extension, where surveillance reforms are usually traded against reauthorization.
